nameStory: The name 'crabweed' likely comes from its sprawling, sideways growth habit that resembles a crab scuttling across the ground. The 'hairy' part refers to the fuzzy texture you'll feel when you touch the leaves and stems, giving this little invader a distinctly soft, velvety feel.
description: Hairy crabweed is a low-growing annual herb that forms small, sprawling patches in disturbed areas. This Asian native belongs to the mulberry family, though it looks nothing like its tree-sized relatives. The plant typically stays under a foot tall, spreading outward with soft, fuzzy stems and leaves that feel almost velvety to the touch. Despite being relatively new to New England, it's gaining a foothold in gardens, greenhouses, and agricultural areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves with toothed edges that feel distinctly soft and fuzzy due to tiny hairs covering the surface - run your finger across one and you'll immediately notice the velvety texture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely getting taller than 8-12 inches but spreading sideways in a crab-like fashion

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Succulent, reddish-green stems covered in the same soft hairs as the leaves, often branching at ground level

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers clustered along the stems - so small you might miss them entirely unless you look closely

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, dark seeds that can stick to clothing and tools, helping explain how this weed spreads so effectively

habitat: Look for hairy crabweed in disturbed soils around gardens, greenhouses, agricultural fields, and other areas where the ground has been recently turned or compacted. It thrives in rich, moist soils and seems particularly fond of cultivated areas where other plants have been disturbed. You're most likely to encounter it in southern New England, though it's slowly spreading northward.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, with young plants appearing as small, fuzzy rosettes in disturbed garden beds and agricultural areas.
seasonality.summer: Plants spread into their characteristic low mats, producing tiny flowers and setting seed throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Continues growing and producing seeds until the first hard frost, when the entire plant dies back as an annual.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent above ground, surviving only as seeds in the soil waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: This innocent-looking little weed is such an effective hitchhiker that it can spread its seeds by sticking to the fur of passing animals, the soles of shoes, and even gardening tools - making every garden visit a potential launching pad for new invasions!
confusionNotes: Its soft, fuzzy texture and sprawling habit might remind you of common chickweed or purslane, but neither of those have the distinctly velvety, hairy feel that gives hairy crabweed its name. If it feels fuzzy to the touch, you've likely found crabweed.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the 'mulberry' family connection fool you - this tiny ground-hugger is completely unrelated to the poison plant called 'crabgrass' and poses no toxicity risk. The mulberry family includes everything from tiny weeds like this to massive fig and mulberry trees.
compareHints: Since hairy crabweed is the only Fatoua species in New England, compare it to other small members of the mulberry family. Unlike the tree-sized mulberries with their large, heart-shaped leaves, crabweed stays tiny with small oval leaves. The key family trait they share is the milky sap you might notice if you break a stem, though it's much less obvious in this small species.
